mcilroy1982.title: Development of a Spelling List
mcilroy1982.author: M. D. McIlroy

mcilroy1982.quote: For the then 25,000-word list hashed into 25,000 16-bit words, or 400,000 bits, the optimal number of hash functions was k = 11, and the probability of false acceptance was less than 1 in 2,000 tries.
quotes: The word list used by the UNIX spelling checker, spell, was developed from many sources over several years.

This paper tells how the spelling checker works, how the words were chosen, how the spelling checker was used to improve itself, and how the (reduced) list of 30,000 English words was squeezed into 26,000 16-bit machine words.
Some years ago, S. C. Johnson introduced the UNIX spelling checker spell.
The spelling list, whose clear text runs to about 250,000 bytes, is accessed randomly.

If the probability of such an error is kept as low as 1 in 2000, then since typical rough drafts rarely have more than 20 bad words, a mistake will be accepted in about 1 in 100 documents, an error rate that is minuscule compared to the incidence of undetectable errors such as an for and or form for from.

Two different hashing methods have been implemented. The first, based on a simple superimposed code scheme first proposed by Bloom, was supplied by D. M. Ritchie and succeeded in encoding a 25,000-word list into 50,000 bytes.
Superimposed coding spatters each entry randomly across a large bit table so thoroughly that the hash values cannot be reconstructed from the table.
Remainders modulo the k largest primes less than N constitute a convenient and effective set of hash functions.

For the then 25,000-word list hashed into 25,000 16-bit words, or 400,000 bits, the optimal number of hash functions was k = 11, and the probability of false acceptance was less than 1 in 2,000 tries.

Experience showed, however, that 25,000 words wasn’t enough; almost every run turned up some worthy new word. To go further, without increasing the hash table size or error rate, the table had to be compressed more tightly.
A desirable vocabulary size for a spelling list is about 30,000, or roughly 2^15 words, a desirable error rate about 1 in 2^12; thus an appropriate hash value size is 27 bits.
How can 2^15 x 27 bits of hash values be jammed into the PDP11’s addressable memory of 2^15 x 16 bits?

If each entry of a v-member vocabulary is hashed into b bits, and only the hash values are remembered, then the probability of false acceptance will be the probability of accidentally hashing into a good value, namely v/2^b.
In our case where v = 30000 and b = 27, this works out to 13.57 bits per entry–small enough to fit!
With a = 2^27/30000 as before, the simple Huffman code given in Appendix C has an expected codeword length of 13.60 bits.
In our case, the expected extra space for breakage and for pointers to 512 bins brings the effective mean codeword length up to 14.01 bits: a tight, but workable fit.
Such codes have been described by Golomb.

To convey maximum information, i.e., to achieve a minimal error rate for a given number of entries, the bits of the table should take values 0 and 1 with equal probability. The probability q of a bit being 0 is q = 1 - (1/N)^km ~ e^(-km/N), where m is the number of entries; q becomes 1/2 when k = (N/m) log 2.
The probability of false acceptance in this instance is (1 - q)^k = 2^-k.
To look up a hash value, one must sum the differences from the beginning until the value sought is reached or surpassed--a time-consuming method indeed.
supports: spell's clear-text word list was about 250,000 bytes
Ritchie supplied the superimposed-code (Bloom) filter: 25,000 words, 400,000 bits, k = 11, false acceptance under 1 in 2,000
false acceptance is tolerable because a rough draft holds ~20 bad words, so one document in 100 lets a mistake through
the 25,000-word list was not enough and the table could not grow without raising the error rate
the exact replacement: 27-bit hash values stored as differences, 13.60 bits per word against a 13.57-bit information-theoretic floor, 14.01 bits effective with 512 bins
the replacement is not error-free: 27-bit hash values give a false-acceptance rate of v/2^b, about 1 in 2^12 (1 in 4,096) at 30,000 words — lower than the filter's 1 in 2,000, at fewer bits per word
McIlroy's own statement of the constraint: to go further "without increasing the hash table size or error rate, the table had to be compressed more tightly"

the Bloom sizing law behind the story's 17.5-bit figure is in this paper, not imported: optimal k = (N/m) log 2 and false acceptance = 2^-k, hence bits per entry N/m = log2(1/p)/ln 2. It reproduces McIlroy's own filter exactly (N/m = 400,000/25,000 = 16 -> k = 11.09 -> 11, p = 2^-11 = 1 in 2,048, 'less than 1 in 2,000'), and at the replacement's error rate p = v/2^b = 30,000/2^27 it gives 17.50 bits per entry against the coded index's 13.57
the coded index is not free: lookup 'must sum the differences from the beginning ... a time-consuming method indeed', which is what the 512 bins and the extra 0.41 bits buy back

v7spellh.title: spell.h, /usr/src/cmd/spell — UNIX Seventh Edition (Research V7) source tree
v7spellh.author: Bell Laboratories
v7spellh.note: Read as raw source from the Research-V7 branch of the unix-history-repo reconstruction. V7 was released January 1979. The file declares `short tab[TABSIZE]` with `#define TABSIZE 25000` and a table `long p[]` of exactly eleven primes: 399871, 399887, 399899, 399911, 399913, 399937, 399941, 399953, 399979, 399983, 399989 — confirmed by computation to be the eleven largest primes below 400,000, which is the paper's 'remainders modulo the k largest primes less than N'. Re-verified 2026-08-22 by a second agent: raw file fetched (HTTP 200); '#define TABSIZE 25000', 'short tab[TABSIZE]' with SHIFT 4 (= 400,000 bits), the eleven-entry long p[] table and the header comment 'a 25000-word dictionary in a 400000-bit table works best with k=11' are all present as recorded.
v7spellh.quote: whence one finds, for example, that a 25000-word dictionary in a 400000-bit table works best with k=11.
quotes: Hash table for spelling checker has n bits. Each word w is hashed by k different (modular) hash functions, hi. The bits hi(w), i=1..k, are set for words in the dictionary.
The probability that a random string is recognized as a word is then (1-P)**k.
#define TABSIZE 25000	/*(int)(400000/(1<<shift))--pdp11 compiler deficiency*/
supports: the superimposed-code filter is not a story about code, it is the code: it shipped in Version 7 Unix
eleven hash functions implemented as remainders modulo the eleven largest primes under 400,000

bloom1970.author: Burton H. Bloom

bloom1970.quote: The reduction in space is accomplished by exploiting the possibility that a small fraction of errors of commission may be tolerable in some applications
quotes: Analysis of the paradigm problem demonstrates that allowing a small number of test messages to be falsely identified as members of the given set will permit a much smaller hash area to be used without increasing reject time.
In application areas where error-free performance is a necessity, these new methods are not applicable.
the size of the hash area (space), the time required to identify a message as a nonmember of the given set (reject time), and an allowable error frequency.
supports: the permitted error is one-directional and Bloom named it: errors of commission
the space saving is bought with, and only with, that permitted error

unverified: The calendar year in which Ritchie's superimposed-code filter was written. The 1982 paper dates neither implementation; the filter is present in the Research V7 tree (V7 released January 1979), which bounds it from above but not below. No year for it appears in the prose.

Whether the differential-coded replacement is properly called 'Golomb coding'. McIlroy's own text calls it a 'differential Huffman code' and an 'infinite Huffman code', and cites Golomb's 1966 run-length encodings paper only as a description of the code family in Appendix C. The prose uses McIlroy's own wording and does not say 'Golomb'.

The dollar cost of PDP-11 memory at Bell Labs at the time. No figure was found in any opened source, so no currency figure appears in the prose; the cost is carried in the machine's own unit, addressable words.

Which Research Unix editions after V7 shipped which of the two methods. The v10spell repository README states its source is 'the spell program from the Tenth Edition Research UNIX system' and that it 'still uses the compressed dictionaries', but this was not traced edition by edition and no such claim appears in the prose.

The year the 25,000-word list actually outgrew the filter. McIlroy reports it only as "experience showed" in the 1982 write-up; it must postdate the filter shipping in V7 (January 1979) but no source narrows it. Card p2c10-c2 is therefore dated 1982, the year of the document that records it, not 1979, which is the year of the cause.

That spell competed for the PDP-11's 32,768 addressable words with other processes. The paper says only "the PDP11's addressable memory of 2^15 x 16 bits" — an address-space limit, not a shared physical pool. The sharing claim was removed from the prose and from card p2c10-c1.

The '~10 bits per item at 1% / ~14.4 at 0.1%' figures are the chapter's own standard Bloom-sizing numbers (body line 85), not McIlroy's, and the story does not attribute the twenty-to-one ratio to him. The comparison figures derived for card p2c10-c4 - 8.1 and 11.4 bits per entry for a coded index at 1% and 0.1%, and the ~10% error rate where the two curves cross - are arithmetic from two formulas that are both in mcilroy1982 (bits per entry for a Bloom filter = log2(1/p)/ln 2; entropy of a set of v hash values of b bits = b - log2(v/e) = log2(1/p) + log2 e), not figures taken from any source. They are reproducible in three lines and were checked against McIlroy's own 13.57 and against his filter's 16 bits at 1 in 2,048, but no publication states them.

An earlier draft of this story and of card p2c10-c4 claimed the two curves cross 'around a tenth of a percent', so that a filter is smaller at 1% and larger at 0.1%. That is wrong and was removed: it held the coded index fixed at McIlroy's 13.57 (which belongs to one error rate, 30,000/2^27) while varying the filter's. At equal error rates the coded index is smaller everywhere below ~10%, and the gap widens as the error target tightens.
